title: How Temper Tantrums Work
summary: Josh and Chuck explain temper tantrums: why they are normal between roughly ages one and four, the role of the prefrontal cortex and its development through adolescence, the fight-or-flight response, and the three stages of a tantrum identified by researcher Michael Potegal. They cover parenting advice such as keeping a schedule, giving choices, ignoring tantrums when safe, and explaining afterward. They discuss breath-holding spells, when tantrums may signal a problem, the DSM-5 addition of disruptive mood dysregulation disorder and its controversy, and teenage tantrums. The episode closes with a listener email about memory loss after a motorcycle crash.

segments.title: Opening banter and parenting advice
segments.summary: The hosts joke about a tantrum and discuss how people judge parents of kids having tantrums, and how parenting advice has shifted over history, from Rousseau onward.

segments.title: Tantrums as normal toddler behavior
segments.summary: Tantrums are common between about ages one and three, with a study finding 91 percent of children aged 30 months to three years had a weekly tantrum. Most kids see a large drop by four or five.

segments.title: Tantrum stages and Michael Potegal's research
segments.summary: Researcher Michael Potegal recorded toddlers and found tantrums last a few minutes, mix sadness and anger, and move through yelling, physical actions, and whimpering. Physical-first tantrums were shorter. Intense screaming can burst capillaries and cause vomiting.

segments.title: Prefrontal cortex and emotional regulation
segments.summary: The prefrontal cortex, which regulates emotion, develops until about age 18 and starts working around age four. Language develops during this time, creating frustration when kids cannot express themselves. Fight-or-flight cortisol responses add to the problem.

segments.title: Preventing tantrums with schedules and choices
segments.summary: Parents can reduce tantrums with a predictable schedule, regular sleep, feeding and interaction, and by giving children choices, such as which pair of shoes to wear.

segments.title: Handling tantrums: ignoring, and explaining afterward
segments.summary: Experts advise ignoring tantrums that are not dangerous, so the child gets no attention, and avoiding punishment during a tantrum. Afterward, parents should calmly explain the problem. The hosts also mention knockoff toys.

segments.title: When tantrums signal a problem: DSM-5 and breath-holding
segments.summary: Three or more tantrums a day lasting over 15 minutes may meet criteria for disruptive mood dysregulation disorder in the DSM-5, which critics question. Pediatric bipolar diagnoses rose sharply and antipsychotic prescriptions for young children doubled. Breath-holding spells are discussed, and home stressors such as moves, divorce or fighting are noted as possible causes.

segments.title: Teenage tantrums and emotional development
segments.summary: The prefrontal cortex develops again during puberty, so teens may show similar outbursts. A University of San Diego study found teens' ability to read facial emotions dropped between ages 10 and 18. The amygdala may take over risk-taking behavior. The hosts also mention a six-year-old girl arrested after a tantrum at school in Militchville.

segments.title: Listener mail: positive amnesia after motorcycle wreck
segments.summary: Adrian writes about a near-fatal motorcycle crash in Portland, Oregon, and the medically induced amnesia that followed, which he says has helped him be less afraid of traffic. The hosts close with contact information.
